issue_assessments.issue: Lawfulness of the August 26 lock change and the condition placed on a new key
issue_assessments.reasoning: Both sides agree Tenant paid no rent for August. That likely permitted an exclusion under Section 93.002(c)(3) and Section 15.2(c). The dispute narrows to the key-release condition: subsection (f) ties the new key to payment of the delinquent rent, and the only record (Tenant's email, substantially confirmed by Landlord's reply) shows a $1,500 fee was also demanded. If that is proven, the exclusion as conducted sits outside the statutory safe harbor. Landlord's fallback, that Section 93.002(h) lets the lease supersede the statute, is weakened because Section 15.2(c) incorporates Section 93.002 rather than displacing it.
unsupported_claims: C1's premise that Landlord 'conditioned' re-entry on the fee relies on an oral telephone exchange recorded only in Tenant's email.
evidence_gaps: Any written statement from Landlord of what was required to obtain the key
procedural_concerns: The writ of reentry procedure in Section 93.003 is time-sensitive and requires a sworn complaint in the justice court for the precinct where the premises are located; justice court rules are not in the library.

issue_assessments.issue: Whether the $1,500 lockout and administrative fee may be assessed
issue_assessments.reasoning: Section 93.012(a) is categorical for charges not stated in the lease. The lease specifies a late charge and attorneys' fees only. Landlord's best response is Section 93.012(b), preserving charges or remedies allowed by statute or common law, but a locksmith cost is more naturally a damages item to be proven than a charge to be imposed as a condition of access. Exhibits B and C were not reviewed and could change this.

refs.quote: A landlord may not assess a charge, excluding a charge for rent or physical damage to the leased premises

issue_assessments.issue: Responsibility for the rooftop HVAC unit and the $8,400 replacement
issue_assessments.reasoning: Section 7.2 ('exclusively serving the Premises') and Section 1.10 ('including rooftop equipment' but 'serving the Building generally') genuinely conflict for a dedicated rooftop unit. Both advocates overstate: C4 treats the Section 2.2 commencement warranty as an ongoing allocation, which it is not on its face; O2 treats 'serving Suite 140' as proof of exclusivity, which the vendor did not actually say. The missing maintenance contract and the end-of-life finding matter to causation. This is a classic ambiguity that a court may resolve with extrinsic evidence; it should be put to counsel.
unsupported_claims: C4: 'Tenant gave written notice on June 10 and June 21' assumes email is notice, contrary to Section 17.2.
O2: 'a dedicated unit does not' serve the Building generally is an inference, not something the lease says.
evidence_gaps: Mechanical drawings or vendor report showing what the rooftop unit serves
The Trinity Mechanical invoice and report

issue_assessments.issue: Whether Tenant's withholding of August rent was permitted
issue_assessments.reasoning: Sections 4.4 and 7.4 are explicit that Rent may not be withheld or offset for a Landlord default, and Section 7.4 prescribes invoice-and-pay rather than deduction. Tenant's argument would require Texas common law to override an express independent-covenant clause, and no authority for that is in the library. Even on Tenant's best view of the HVAC issue, the chosen remedy was the wrong one under the lease.
unsupported_claims: Any suggestion that an 'emergency' excused the no-offset clause lacks support in the lease text.
evidence_gaps: Case law on independent-covenant clauses in Texas commercial leases (not in library)

issue_assessments.issue: Whether a lease Event of Default had matured before the lock change
issue_assessments.reasoning: Everything turns on proof of certified mailing on or about August 11. If mailed, deemed delivery three business days later plus ten days expires on or about August 24, before August 26, and C3 fails. If not mailed, the only notice was email, Section 17.2 says email is not notice, and the cure period arguably never began. Tenant's August 26 reference to 'the August 11 email attachment' is a plausible but not certain written acknowledgment. Note the statutory lock-change right in Section 93.002(c)(3) does not itself depend on the lease's notice mechanics, so this issue affects lease remedies more than the statutory analysis.
unsupported_claims: O4's statement that Tenant's August 26 email 'supplies the written acknowledgment' is an interpretation, not a documented fact.
evidence_gaps: Original email headers showing when the notice attachment was received
procedural_concerns: Section 17.1's deemed-delivery rule may shift the burden; counsel should assess who must prove mailing.

refs.quote: three (3) business days after deposit in the United States mail, certified, return receipt requested

unsupported_interpretations.problem: Treats Section 2.2's commencement-date representation as an allocation of ongoing repair responsibility; the clause speaks only to condition at delivery.
Assumes actual receipt is required for notice; Section 17.1(c) deems notice given three business days after certified mailing.
Infers that the unit serves only Suite 140 from the phrase 'serving Suite 140'; the vendor's report in the file does not say 'exclusively'.
Asserts the posted notice satisfied Section 93.002(f) without addressing that the key was conditioned on a fee beyond delinquent rent.

conflicting_provisions.description: Section 1.10 includes rooftop equipment in Building Systems (Landlord), while Section 7.2 assigns HVAC exclusively serving the Premises to Tenant. A dedicated rooftop unit fits both descriptions.

Section 15.2(c) permits a lock change 'upon an Event of Default' (which requires notice and ten days), while the incorporated statute permits a lock change for mere delinquency. Which standard governs the August 26 action is unresolved.

overall_commentary: The customer's position is strongest on how the lockout was carried out (the fee and the key condition) and weakest on the decision to withhold rent. The HVAC allocation is a genuine ambiguity on which reasonable readers differ. Several conclusions depend on documents not in the file, especially proof of mailing and the vendor invoice, and should be treated as open until those are produced.
